Pat Lambie - the babyfaced assassin retires

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
The decision by charismatic Sharks and Springbok flyhalf and fullback Pat Lambie to retire from professional rugby at the age of 28 has focused attention sharply on the problem of concussion in professional contact sport – especially rugby. He played 56 matches for South Africa.

Summary:
Lambie, who is currently contracted to French club, Racing 92, said on Saturday he was retiring on medical advice, telling French news outlet Le Equipe that he had already contemplated retirement before arriving in France after three concussions in South Africa, "two of them serious." After the last, in May 2017, he didn’t play for six months.
He suffered a further concussion in December 2017. The symptoms lasted 40 days. He said that the repeat concussions had caused “trembling legs, headaches, migraines and eye irritations. I have not been able to do any weight sessions in the last two and a half months because I had a terrible headache.
“I followed the advice of two neurologists. They advised me to stop rugby.”
The 28-year-old spent several months out of the game after taking a horrible knock to his head in a collision with South African-born Ireland flank CJ Stander in a Test at Newlands in June 2016.
He struggled with concussion-related symptoms since that incident and again suffered a heavy head knock when he collided with Sharks team-mate Rhyno Smith during a Super Rugby clash against the Southern Kings in May 2017.
Lambie is widely regarded as one of South Africa’s most talented backline players in recent history because despite his relatively small stature – 86kg, and 1.77m – he is able to play at just about any backline position, switching easily from flyhalf to fullback, and is a deadly kicker.

Further information:
His Sharks and Bok team mate, Tendai Beast Mtawarira wrote on Twitter, "Gutted to hear of your premature retirement brother @PatLambie great player, great career, great teammate and a better friend. All the best with the next chapter".
But what his retirement has really done is to sharply focus attention on concussion in professional contact sport.

Rob Houwing, Chief Writer for Sport24 and one of SA’s leading rugby commentators, describes him as being a “merciless assassin behind his baby face” and says that “Lambie is modest, obliging, responsible, serene, softly smiling … add to those behaviourally-linked hallmarks the range of backline berths where you could be close to certain he’d do a competent job at very worst, and you were really looking at the model tourist, weren’t you?
“How cruel and ironic, then, that entirely justified, clearly mounting concerns about the volume and severity of head knocks he has suffered in his rugby career forced him to pull the plug on it at the age of 28, when he might instead - and perhaps with the benefit he wasn’t enjoying of greater on-field continuity - be at his prime. Those closest to him, in particular, are likely to be relieved, an emotion that will help wash down the doubtless widespread regret.”
“Perhaps (the Lambie memory that is) most memorable, rugby-orthodox one is his game-deciding, beyond-comfort-zone penalty kick against the All Blacks, hitherto on a run of 22 unbeaten fixtures, at Ellis Park in 2014. He had only been on the park for quarter of an hour, having replaced Handre Pollard at pivot, when the Springboks, behind the halfway line, were awarded a tantalising, 78th-minute penalty. His body language extraordinarily assured considering the magnitude of the kick, Lambie hit it straight as a knife and cleared the crossbar with plenty to spare, to the near-demented delight of the Johannesburg crowd as the Boks earned a famous 27-25 victory.
“It was an example of the extent of inner strength lurking just beneath the baby face.”
Director of Sports Concussions South Africa, Dr Jon Patricios says the recorded incidence of concussions in rugby has increased considerably over the last 10 years but to keep in mind that there is also an increased awareness and diagnosis techniques have improved.
“We have to be careful in interpreting those statistics because we are also on the lookout for concussions far more than we were before. So we are noting concussions a lot more and our criteria for diagnosing concussions are far broader than they were and the fact that we are picking these up more than we were in the past is a positive outcome.
“In the past, a lot of these injuries were ignored and some of the tackling mechanisms that led to concussions weren't punished. The law changes that have come into place in the last couple of years have certainly had a significant impact in reducing the types of high tackles and contact situations which may lead to more serious head and neck injuries.”
It has also been asked whether or not head injuries may have been a cause of Joost van der Westhuizen’s deadly motor neuron disease – and it has also been suggested that repeat concussions can lead to Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy and other neurological diseases.
These include Andre Venter, who suffers from a degenerative nervous condition called transverse myelitis, and other MND victis, including Tinus Linee, who died of MND in 2014 aged 45; New Zealand rugby union fullback Jarrod Cunningham who died of the disease in 2007; ex-Sharks rugby player Ryan Walker who was diagnosed with MND at the age of 35; and former Natal wing Danny Delport, who was diagnosed in 2014. Another famous sufferer of motor neuron disease is American baseball legend Lou Gehrig, after whom the most common MND, Lou Gehrig's Disease, was named.
Experts say that between 5 and 10 percent of MND is genetic. The other 90-odd percent is down to environmental factors, of which regular concussions is one. Another disease is traumatic encephalopthy, “punch-drunk disease”.
First demonstrated in boxers as "punch-drunk disease", CTE results from repeated, mild head trauma as a result of blows to the skull. Collectively, these individually rather minor brain injuries can cause progressive damage to nerve cells and changes in the brain that ultimately lead to a slew of cognitive, emotional, behavioural and physical problems, many of which may only become apparent years later.
CTE shares similarities with other degenerative illnesses such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease and Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Typical symptoms include short-term memory loss, depression, irritability, aggressiveness and suicidal tendencies. Currently the disease can only be diagnosed after death.
In the United States, CTE has been associated predominantly with professional ice hockey and American football players, but increasingly also with other sports, including soccer, rugby, wrestling and field hockey.
But there is some controversy around it, with a 2014 article by Jon Patricios and Dr Simon Kemp in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, pointed out that CTE has gained a lot of notoriety on social media networks and through high-profile lawsuits “in spite of an absence of evidence of established risks”.
They recommended further research into the field, arguing that “as physicians and scientists, we need to reclaim clinical decision making from the realm of media-driven and often frenzied public opinion”.
A paper published in the Quarterly Journal of Medicine in May 2015 suggests that “the association between exposure to head injury and increased risk of neurodegenerative disease, specifically chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), is widely recognised”, and that “it is clear that it is the exposure to head injury which is associated with increased dementia risk, and not the circumstances or environment of exposure".
The implication is that CTE may not only be a problem in boxing, but also in those sports in which blows to the head are less frequent and usually accidental.
What does the rule book say about concussion in rugby?
Regulation 10 of the World Rugby (formerly IRB) code says that any player suspected of concussion must be taken off and not allowed back on to the field during the match.
There is an exception to the rule that applies to players in elite adult matches, series of matches or tournaments that have been approved in advance by World Rugby. If they are suspected of having suffered concussion and can pass a series of tests lasting five minutes the player can be allowed back into the game.
It’s known as the Head Injury Assessment (formerly PSCA/Pitch Side Concussion Assessment) or the five-minute rule. It is said to be 84.6% accurate in determining concussion.
Barry O’Driscoll, a former medical adviser to the International Rugby Board, resigned in 2012 over what he saw as a reckless stance on concussion – referring to the introduction of the controversial five-minute concussion bin.
"We are sending concussed players back onto the field – brain damaged players," he said. "We know now what's going on in the brain as soon as it is hit. The glucose metabolism, the oxygen uptake, the electrolytes ... are all thrown completely out. This is a brain in disarray. It's not functioning properly.
"The decision making is reduced, the cognitive function is reduced, and the emotions are thrown. What on earth is a person in that state going back onto the rugby field for?"

Press Release:


Pat Lambie
A concussion is a dangerous head injury and in rugby, high tackles can have a devastating outcome. Despite World rugby tightening regulations around tackling and contact to the head, concussion rates are still high. Now Springbok, Pat Lambie’s early retirement after several serious concussions has rugby fans and sports specialists abuzz. Can more be done to make the sport safer?
Producer: Liz Fish
Presenter: Derek Watts
Watch the trailer


Script:


Script: This was the beginning of the end of Pat Lambie’s rugby career- Newlands 2016- CJ Stander attempted to charge down a clearance kick by Lambie, striking him square in the face, and knocking him out stone cold for 20 minutes
Pat: Since 2016 I've had four concussions and with all of them I have suffered from these post-concussion symptoms and now it seems as though every time I do have a big trauma to my head it takes me longer and longer to shake off these symptoms
Link: It must have been one of the toughest decision to make for a professional player at the peak of his career – retire or risk permanent brain damage.
Script: Pat Lambie suffered a knee injury in April last year while playing in France for Racing 92, everyone was anticipating seeing him back in play early this year. But then came his shocking announcement that he was retiring from rugby.
Pat: The last few months it's been a long journey a big process that has had to unfold and obviously gutted and hugely disappointed to have to step away from a game that I love so much. But in the same breath I'm feeling quite relieved that I know my health is not at risk any further and there's no chance of receiving any more serious head injuries
Link: Pat Lambie retirement at the age of 28 at peak of his career has once again brought into sharp focus the problem of concussion in a contact sport
Pat: We're at nine months now since my last head knock and I've still got these symptoms. So I wake up in the morning feeling quite groggy my eyes are extremely sensitive to light sensitive screens. If I do a heavy weights session they start stinging. The specialists are all saying that we don't know what will happen if I get another hard impact and how long these symptoms will last for after that one. So it's best that I stop playing.
Link: “Pat Lambie burst onto the first class rugby stage when he was just 19 here in Durban stealing the hearts of rugby fans. It wasn’t long before commentators recognised his enormous talent and started calling him the baby faced assassin
Script: He was the youngest member of the Springboks’ Rugby World Cup squad in 2011, and went on to play 56 Tests and two tour matches. He left the Sharks and Springboks in 2017 to join the French club Racing 92
Script: Stefan Terblanche Captained the Sharks in 2010 in the Currie Cup Final when Lambie played the game that made his history
Stef: I sent him a message early in the morning in a most diplomatic Pat Lambie way. He basically sent one back. Don't worry about me old man. I'll make sure I arrive at the game. Derek: Old Man. Stef: Yeah exactly. And two tries 25 points later. You know he was man of the match and also got selected for the Springbok team that evening.
Pat: That was one of the best days of my life. I think to be involved in the Sharks team that won the Currie Cup Final and then to come off the field and see that I was included in the end of year Springbok touring squad was just all almost too much to take in
Script: His team mate, Tendai Beast Mtawarira, was gutted by Lambie retirement.
Tendai: I think Pat epitomized what it means to be a professional sportsman. You know he really handled himself really well and always trained very hard and treated everybody around him with respect and I drew a lot of inspiration from him.
Script: Another standout moment was his game-deciding, penalty kick against the All Blacks at Ellis Park in 2014. Up until then the All Blacks had an unbeaten 22 games, and Lambie’s kick, earned the Boks the famous 27-25 victory.
Pat: And the atmosphere at Ellis Park that day was something that I will never ever forget. And it was it was an amazing experience to be a part of that win and to be a little part of it
Script: But his career began to be plagued by concussion. After the first one in 2016, there were 3 more, but his decision to play on after the last concussion, seems to have done the damage
Pat “I didn’t want to go off the field obviously because the semi-final it was a big occasion. It wasn't a very wise decision for me to have continued playing at that point. Luckily enough for me it was in the next game only three minutes in that I hurt my knee and I have never played since
Link: One of the reasons rugby is so exciting to watch is because it’s an extremely physical game. But in the last year alone 6 players have died globally.
Script: And Concussion is the most common injury suffered by rugby players, and the stats have risen every year for the last seven. Some say it’s as bad as boxing. Professor Jon Patricios founder and Director of Sports Concussion South Africa, is a consultant to World Rugby
Jon: I think the exposure of our players is much more than it was even 10 or 15 years ago the players are bigger they're faster they're the contacts are greater and more frequent. The ball is in play more often and they're playing more frequently. There's no such thing as a rugby season anymore and it's a 12 month of the year process.
Link: A recent report found that the international rules regarding contact to the head have had little or no effect when it comes to the frequency of concussion
Script: Pat Lambie is the latest international rugby player who has been forced to retire because of concussion - Mike Blair Scotland, Jonathan Thomas Wales, Andy Hazell England, Ben Afeaki New Zealand, Elton Flatley Australia.
Script: World Rugby has made huge strides to improve the safety of the game since Stefan Terblanche’s day, he played professionally between ‘94 to 2012
Stef: A lot of guys got concussed there were no head injury assessments and and really didn't take the necessary precaution and played the next weekend. So yes we got concussed got and carried on.
Jon: Up sound So you might get hit on the back of the head but the damage is at the front……….
Jon: If you think back 15, 20 years ago we were missing a lot of concussions. Now we now we realise a whole ambit of at least 20 symptoms and signs that we look out for that might indicate a potential concussion.
Derek: Now the beast isn’t afraid of some robust play. Do you ever worry about head injuries?
Tendai: I do, but I guess you know the training that we do in the conditioning kind of prepares us for that. You know for those hard collisions we take on the field but you know there's a way you know rugby is protected you know so you can really take a guy you know upstairs or above the neck so you always know that the law kind of protects you.
Stef: These days the rules have changed no contact from the shoulders above up when players do make contact with the head of an opposing player the sanctions are quite severe from anything from four to six to eight to 12 weeks that you're not allowed to play.
Script: Most people recover fully from concussion with rest and physiotherapy, Megyn Robertson helped Pat enormously
Megyn: We managed to alleviate some of his difficulty tracking the ball and his balance improved so you can sidestep more quickly and feel more confident going into a tackle and just basically relieve some of his neck pain symptoms because he often had a really tight congested neck. The difficulty with Pat is that he had an underlying migraine history that keeps tripping up the concussion symptoms.
Pat “It's really really nice that there are things that can be done to get on top of these symptoms and it's not just a waiting game.
Link : The pressure to win and stay in the game is enormous players feel they have to man up and play through the pain head injuries are difficult to see and in many way harder to admit to
Pat: “There's this mentality that you should man up and play on and that a concussion or a head injury is not such a big deal. People will forgive you for coming off if you've broken your ankle or popped your ac joint in your shoulder you can be seen to be walking around for the next few weeks with crutches. The scans and results can all be clear but actually you know there are consequences inside your head and everyone will look at you and think you're absolutely fine but you're not feeling yourself. And eventually people can start asking questions
Stef: There expectations of the supporters of the crowd and of yourself to win the game. So more often than not you go onto the field with a slight niggle you know take a painkiller get injection numb the pain and you play through it. A Head injury doesn't quite work like that. Yes you might run off the headache but the long term ramifications could be brutal.
Script: Lambie blazed a trail through rugby history with his legendary kicks and extraordinary tries. Everyone is sad to see this shining star burn out so soon.
Pat: Emotionally it has been a real roller coaster. I'm not exactly sure what the future holds at the moment. We are obviously expecting a little baby in June so that's something really exciting to look forward to. It's been an incredible almost 10 year journey and one that I'll look back on for the rest of my life with really really fond memories. So thank you to everyone that's been involved.
Stef: From all of us. I think certainly from the shark's family thank you so much for everything that you've given the game still you've still got a whole lot more to offer and it was an absolute privilege playing with you in the same jersey.
Tendai: You know I just want to say that now you know you left an everlasting mark in the game and you're definitely one of the best who have ever played the game. Thank you for the inspiration you brought to a lot of us to the Sharks to the youngsters out there you know dream of playing professional rugby. Now you're a great role model buddy.

from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 03 February 2019 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 15 March 2019 Press Release: Pat Lambie A concussion is a dangerous head injury and in rugby, high tackles can have a devastating outcome. Despite World rugby tightening regulations around tackling and contact to the head, concussion rates are still high. Now Springbok, Pat Lambie’s early retirement after several serious concussions has rugby fans and sports specialists abuzz. Can more be done to make the sport safer? Producer: Liz Fish Presenter: Derek Watts Watch the trailer Script: Script: This was the beginning of the end of Pat Lambie’s rugby career- Newlands 2016- CJ Stander attempted to charge down a clearance kick by Lambie, striking him square in the face, and knocking him out stone cold for 20 minutes Pat: Since 2016 I've had four concussions and with all of them I have suffered from these post-concussion symptoms and now it seems as though every time I do have a big trauma to my head it takes me longer and longer to shake off these symptoms Link: It must have been one of the toughest decision to make for a professional player at the peak of his career – retire or risk permanent brain damage. Script: Pat Lambie suffered a knee injury in April last year while playing in France for Racing 92, everyone was anticipating seeing him back in play early this year. But then came his shocking announcement that he was retiring from rugby. Pat: The last few months it's been a long journey a big process that has had to unfold and obviously gutted and hugely disappointed to have to step away from a game that I love so much. But in the same breath I'm feeling quite relieved that I know my health is not at risk any further and there's no chance of receiving any more serious head injuries Link: Pat Lambie retirement at the age of 28 at peak of his career has once again brought into sharp focus the problem of concussion in a contact sport Pat: We're at nine months now since my last head knock and I've still got these symptoms. So I wake up in the morning feeling quite groggy my eyes are extremely sensitive to light sensitive screens. If I do a heavy weights session they start stinging. The specialists are all saying that we don't know what will happen if I get another hard impact and how long these symptoms will last for after that one. So it's best that I stop playing. Link: “Pat Lambie burst onto the first class rugby stage when he was just 19 here in Durban stealing the hearts of rugby fans. It wasn’t long before commentators recognised his enormous talent and started calling him the baby faced assassin Script: He was the youngest member of the Springboks’ Rugby World Cup squad in 2011, and went on to play 56 Tests and two tour matches. He left the Sharks and Springboks in 2017 to join the French club Racing 92 Script: Stefan Terblanche Captained the Sharks in 2010 in the Currie Cup Final when Lambie played the game that made his history Stef: I sent him a message early in the morning in a most diplomatic Pat Lambie way. He basically sent one back. Don't worry about me old man. I'll make sure I arrive at the game. Derek: Old Man. Stef: Yeah exactly. And two tries 25 points later. You know he was man of the match and also got selected for the Springbok team that evening. Pat: That was one of the best days of my life. I think to be involved in the Sharks team that won the Currie Cup Final and then to come off the field and see that I was included in the end of year Springbok touring squad was just all almost too much to take in Script: His team mate, Tendai Beast Mtawarira, was gutted by Lambie retirement. Tendai: I think Pat epitomized what it means to be a professional sportsman. You know he really handled himself really well and always trained very hard and treated everybody around him with respect and I drew a lot of inspiration from him. Script: Another standout moment was his game-deciding, penalty kick against the All Blacks at Ellis Park in 2014. Up until then the All Blacks had an unbeaten 22 games, and Lambie’s kick, earned the Boks the famous 27-25 victory. Pat: And the atmosphere at Ellis Park that day was something that I will never ever forget. And it was it was an amazing experience to be a part of that win and to be a little part of it Script: But his career began to be plagued by concussion. After the first one in 2016, there were 3 more, but his decision to play on after the last concussion, seems to have done the damage Pat “I didn’t want to go off the field obviously because the semi-final it was a big occasion. It wasn't a very wise decision for me to have continued playing at that point. Luckily enough for me it was in the next game only three minutes in that I hurt my knee and I have never played since Link: One of the reasons rugby is so exciting to watch is because it’s an extremely physical game. But in the last year alone 6 players have died globally. Script: And Concussion is the most common injury suffered by rugby players, and the stats have risen every year for the last seven. Some say it’s as bad as boxing. Professor Jon Patricios founder and Director of Sports Concussion South Africa, is a consultant to World Rugby Jon: I think the exposure of our players is much more than it was even 10 or 15 years ago the players are bigger they're faster they're the contacts are greater and more frequent. The ball is in play more often and they're playing more frequently. There's no such thing as a rugby season anymore and it's a 12 month of the year process. Link: A recent report found that the international rules regarding contact to the head have had little or no effect when it comes to the frequency of concussion Script: Pat Lambie is the latest international rugby player who has been forced to retire because of concussion - Mike Blair Scotland, Jonathan Thomas Wales, Andy Hazell England, Ben Afeaki New Zealand, Elton Flatley Australia. Script: World Rugby has made huge strides to improve the safety of the game since Stefan Terblanche’s day, he played professionally between ‘94 to 2012 Stef: A lot of guys got concussed there were no head injury assessments and and really didn't take the necessary precaution and played the next weekend. So yes we got concussed got and carried on. Jon: Up sound So you might get hit on the back of the head but the damage is at the front………. Jon: If you think back 15, 20 years ago we were missing a lot of concussions. Now we now we realise a whole ambit of at least 20 symptoms and signs that we look out for that might indicate a potential concussion. Derek: Now the beast isn’t afraid of some robust play. Do you ever worry about head injuries? Tendai: I do, but I guess you know the training that we do in the conditioning kind of prepares us for that. You know for those hard collisions we take on the field but you know there's a way you know rugby is protected you know so you can really take a guy you know upstairs or above the neck so you always know that the law kind of protects you. Stef: These days the rules have changed no contact from the shoulders above up when players do make contact with the head of an opposing player the sanctions are quite severe from anything from four to six to eight to 12 weeks that you're not allowed to play. Script: Most people recover fully from concussion with rest and physiotherapy, Megyn Robertson helped Pat enormously Megyn: We managed to alleviate some of his difficulty tracking the ball and his balance improved so you can sidestep more quickly and feel more confident going into a tackle and just basically relieve some of his neck pain symptoms because he often had a really tight congested neck. The difficulty with Pat is that he had an underlying migraine history that keeps tripping up the concussion symptoms. Pat “It's really really nice that there are things that can be done to get on top of these symptoms and it's not just a waiting game. Link : The pressure to win and stay in the game is enormous players feel they have to man up and play through the pain head injuries are difficult to see and in many way harder to admit to Pat: “There's this mentality that you should man up and play on and that a concussion or a head injury is not such a big deal. People will forgive you for coming off if you've broken your ankle or popped your ac joint in your shoulder you can be seen to be walking around for the next few weeks with crutches. The scans and results can all be clear but actually you know there are consequences inside your head and everyone will look at you and think you're absolutely fine but you're not feeling yourself. And eventually people can start asking questions Stef: There expectations of the supporters of the crowd and of yourself to win the game. So more often than not you go onto the field with a slight niggle you know take a painkiller get injection numb the pain and you play through it. A Head injury doesn't quite work like that. Yes you might run off the headache but the long term ramifications could be brutal. Script: Lambie blazed a trail through rugby history with his legendary kicks and extraordinary tries. Everyone is sad to see this shining star burn out so soon. Pat: Emotionally it has been a real roller coaster. I'm not exactly sure what the future holds at the moment. We are obviously expecting a little baby in June so that's something really exciting to look forward to. It's been an incredible almost 10 year journey and one that I'll look back on for the rest of my life with really really fond memories. So thank you to everyone that's been involved. Stef: From all of us. I think certainly from the shark's family thank you so much for everything that you've given the game still you've still got a whole lot more to offer and it was an absolute privilege playing with you in the same jersey. Tendai: You know I just want to say that now you know you left an everlasting mark in the game and you're definitely one of the best who have ever played the game. Thank you for the inspiration you brought to a lot of us to the Sharks to the youngsters out there you know dream of playing professional rugby. Now you're a great role model buddy. metadata.Unique Selling Point: The decision by charismatic Sharks and Springbok flyhalf and fullback Pat Lambie to retire from professional rugby at the age of 28 has focused attention sharply on the problem of concussion in professional contact sport – especially rugby. He played 56 matches for South Africa.
metadata.Summary: Lambie, who is currently contracted to French club, Racing 92, said on Saturday he was retiring on medical advice, telling French news outlet Le Equipe that he had already contemplated retirement before arriving in France after three concussions in South Africa, "two of them serious." After the last, in May 2017, he didn’t play for six months. He suffered a further concussion in December 2017. The symptoms lasted 40 days. He said that the repeat concussions had caused “trembling legs, headaches, migraines and eye irritations. I have not been able to do any weight sessions in the last two and a half months because I had a terrible headache. “I followed the advice of two neurologists. They advised me to stop rugby.” The 28-year-old spent several months out of the game after taking a horrible knock to his head in a collision with South African-born Ireland flank CJ Stander in a Test at Newlands in June 2016. He struggled with concussion-related symptoms since that incident and again suffered a heavy head knock when he collided with Sharks team-mate Rhyno Smith during a Super Rugby clash against the Southern Kings in May 2017. Lambie is widely regarded as one of South Africa’s most talented backline players in recent history because despite his relatively small stature – 86kg, and 1.77m – he is able to play at just about any backline position, switching easily from flyhalf to fullback, and is a deadly kicker.
metadata.Further information: His Sharks and Bok team mate, Tendai Beast Mtawarira wrote on Twitter, "Gutted to hear of your premature retirement brother @PatLambie great player, great career, great teammate and a better friend. All the best with the next chapter". But what his retirement has really done is to sharply focus attention on concussion in professional contact sport. Rob Houwing, Chief Writer for Sport24 and one of SA’s leading rugby commentators, describes him as being a “merciless assassin behind his baby face” and says that “Lambie is modest, obliging, responsible, serene, softly smiling … add to those behaviourally-linked hallmarks the range of backline berths where you could be close to certain he’d do a competent job at very worst, and you were really looking at the model tourist, weren’t you? “How cruel and ironic, then, that entirely justified, clearly mounting concerns about the volume and severity of head knocks he has suffered in his rugby career forced him to pull the plug on it at the age of 28, when he might instead - and perhaps with the benefit he wasn’t enjoying of greater on-field continuity - be at his prime. Those closest to him, in particular, are likely to be relieved, an emotion that will help wash down the doubtless widespread regret.” “Perhaps (the Lambie memory that is) most memorable, rugby-orthodox one is his game-deciding, beyond-comfort-zone penalty kick against the All Blacks, hitherto on a run of 22 unbeaten fixtures, at Ellis Park in 2014. He had only been on the park for quarter of an hour, having replaced Handre Pollard at pivot, when the Springboks, behind the halfway line, were awarded a tantalising, 78th-minute penalty. His body language extraordinarily assured considering the magnitude of the kick, Lambie hit it straight as a knife and cleared the crossbar with plenty to spare, to the near-demented delight of the Johannesburg crowd as the Boks earned a famous 27-25 victory. “It was an example of the extent of inner strength lurking just beneath the baby face.” Director of Sports Concussions South Africa, Dr Jon Patricios says the recorded incidence of concussions in rugby has increased considerably over the last 10 years but to keep in mind that there is also an increased awareness and diagnosis techniques have improved. “We have to be careful in interpreting those statistics because we are also on the lookout for concussions far more than we were before. So we are noting concussions a lot more and our criteria for diagnosing concussions are far broader than they were and the fact that we are picking these up more than we were in the past is a positive outcome. “In the past, a lot of these injuries were ignored and some of the tackling mechanisms that led to concussions weren't punished. The law changes that have come into place in the last couple of years have certainly had a significant impact in reducing the types of high tackles and contact situations which may lead to more serious head and neck injuries.” It has also been asked whether or not head injuries may have been a cause of Joost van der Westhuizen’s deadly motor neuron disease – and it has also been suggested that repeat concussions can lead to Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy and other neurological diseases. These include Andre Venter, who suffers from a degenerative nervous condition called transverse myelitis, and other MND victis, including Tinus Linee, who died of MND in 2014 aged 45; New Zealand rugby union fullback Jarrod Cunningham who died of the disease in 2007; ex-Sharks rugby player Ryan Walker who was diagnosed with MND at the age of 35; and former Natal wing Danny Delport, who was diagnosed in 2014. Another famous sufferer of motor neuron disease is American baseball legend Lou Gehrig, after whom the most common MND, Lou Gehrig's Disease, was named. Experts say that between 5 and 10 percent of MND is genetic. The other 90-odd percent is down to environmental factors, of which regular concussions is one. Another disease is traumatic encephalopthy, “punch-drunk disease”. First demonstrated in boxers as "punch-drunk disease", CTE results from repeated, mild head trauma as a result of blows to the skull. Collectively, these individually rather minor brain injuries can cause progressive damage to nerve cells and changes in the brain that ultimately lead to a slew of cognitive, emotional, behavioural and physical problems, many of which may only become apparent years later. CTE shares similarities with other degenerative illnesses such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease and Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Typical symptoms include short-term memory loss, depression, irritability, aggressiveness and suicidal tendencies. Currently the disease can only be diagnosed after death. In the United States, CTE has been associated predominantly with professional ice hockey and American football players, but increasingly also with other sports, including soccer, rugby, wrestling and field hockey. But there is some controversy around it, with a 2014 article by Jon Patricios and Dr Simon Kemp in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, pointed out that CTE has gained a lot of notoriety on social media networks and through high-profile lawsuits “in spite of an absence of evidence of established risks”. They recommended further research into the field, arguing that “as physicians and scientists, we need to reclaim clinical decision making from the realm of media-driven and often frenzied public opinion”. A paper published in the Quarterly Journal of Medicine in May 2015 suggests that “the association between exposure to head injury and increased risk of neurodegenerative disease, specifically chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), is widely recognised”, and that “it is clear that it is the exposure to head injury which is associated with increased dementia risk, and not the circumstances or environment of exposure". The implication is that CTE may not only be a problem in boxing, but also in those sports in which blows to the head are less frequent and usually accidental. What does the rule book say about concussion in rugby? Regulation 10 of the World Rugby (formerly IRB) code says that any player suspected of concussion must be taken off and not allowed back on to the field during the match. There is an exception to the rule that applies to players in elite adult matches, series of matches or tournaments that have been approved in advance by World Rugby. If they are suspected of having suffered concussion and can pass a series of tests lasting five minutes the player can be allowed back into the game. It’s known as the Head Injury Assessment (formerly PSCA/Pitch Side Concussion Assessment) or the five-minute rule. It is said to be 84.6% accurate in determining concussion. Barry O’Driscoll, a former medical adviser to the International Rugby Board, resigned in 2012 over what he saw as a reckless stance on concussion – referring to the introduction of the controversial five-minute concussion bin. "We are sending concussed players back onto the field – brain damaged players," he said. "We know now what's going on in the brain as soon as it is hit. The glucose metabolism, the oxygen uptake, the electrolytes ... are all thrown completely out. This is a brain in disarray. It's not functioning properly. "The decision making is reduced, the cognitive function is reduced, and the emotions are thrown. What on earth is a person in that state going back onto the rugby field for?"
